name: Linux — Anti-Forensics: File Immutability or Secure Deletion (chattr/shred)
description: Detects execution of chattr (setting/removing file immutability, often to protect malware or block log writes) or secure-deletion tools (shred/wipe/srm) used to destroy forensic evidence.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. `chattr +i` protects a file from modification; `shred` destroys it.
## Response
Preserve remaining evidence, identify the target files, and treat as active intrusion cleanup.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("chattr" or "shred" or "wipe" or "srm")

name: Linux — at/batch Job Scheduling (Persistence)
description: Detects use of the 'at' / 'batch' one-shot job schedulers (0 baseline on these servers), used by attackers to schedule delayed or one-time execution of payloads for persistence or defence evasion.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` scheduled a job via at/batch on `host.name`.
2. Inspect the scheduled command (atq/at -c).
## Response
Remove unauthorised jobs and investigate the user.
author: raadabujaish

name: Linux — Container Escape Tooling Executed (nsenter/unshare/capsh)
description: Detects execution of namespace/capability manipulation tools (nsenter, unshare, capsh) commonly used to break out of a container to the host or to manipulate Linux namespaces for privilege escalation.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` on `host.name` ran `process.executable` with `process.args`.
2. Determine whether the host is a container node and whether the invocation targets the host namespace/PID 1.
## Response
If unexpected, isolate the node and inspect the originating container/pod.
author: raadabujaish

name: Linux — Netcat/Socat Execution (Reverse Shell / Tunneling)
description: Detects execution of netcat/socat — frequently used to establish reverse shells, bind shells, or data-tunneling channels. These tools do not appear in normal application workloads on these servers.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. Look for `-e`, `exec`, or `/dev/tcp` patterns and the remote endpoint.
## Response
Isolate the host and identify the C2 destination and parent process.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.category:"process" and process.name:("nc" or "ncat" or "netcat" or "socat")

name: Linux — pkexec Execution (PwnKit / Local Privilege Escalation)
description: Detects execution of pkexec, the setuid Polkit binary abused by PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) and related local privilege-escalation exploits to obtain root. pkexec is not used by normal workloads on these servers (0 baseline).
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. PwnKit exploitation often shows pkexec with empty/malformed argv and an unusual parent.
## Response
If unexpected, isolate the host, patch Polkit, and hunt for root-level persistence.
author: raadabujaish

name: Linux — Scripted Password Change (chpasswd)
description: Detects execution of chpasswd, which sets account passwords non-interactively from a script or pipe — used by attackers to change or reset local account passwords for persistence or account takeover.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran chpasswd on `host.name`.
2. Identify which account(s) had passwords changed.
## Response
Verify authorisation; if malicious, reset affected accounts and investigate.
author: raadabujaish

name: Linux — SELinux / Security Control Tampering (setenforce/semanage)
description: Detects execution of setenforce or semanage, used to place SELinux in permissive mode or alter its policy — a common step to disable a Linux security control before further attack activity.
note:
## Investigation
1. `user.name` ran `process.executable` `process.args` on `host.name`.
2. `setenforce 0` disables SELinux enforcement.
## Response
Re-enable enforcement, and investigate what activity followed the change.
author: raadabujaish
